name: Nanofat / fat grafting tear trough

card.summary: The patient's own fat, moved into under-eye hollows; longer-lasting in theory, with sparse tear-trough-specific trial data.
card.aka: Autologous fat transfer, lipofilling, periorbital fat grafting
card.note: Fat necrosis, reabsorption and contour irregularities are documented; embolic complications are described with autologous fat.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting takes fat from elsewhere on the body, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas that have lost volume. In the under-eye region it is used to soften hollows where the lower eyelid meets the cheek. Nanofat refers to fat that has been broken down into a finer emulsion, which proponents describe as useful for thin skin.

It is a surgical procedure rather than a product, and it is discussed in appearance communities as an alternative to hyaluronic acid filler because the material is the patient's own tissue. Published tear-trough-specific trials are scarce.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested, handled to preserve cell survival, and re-injected into the target area to add volume. Some of it is reabsorbed, and reports describe stem-cell-related regenerative effects as a rationale for finer preparations such as nanofat.
quick.risks: Reported risks include swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, infection, lumps or contour irregularity, fat necrosis and variable reabsorption. Embolic complications, including rare vision loss, are described with injectable materials and have been linked more often to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.

lead: Fat grafting, also called autologous fat transfer or lipofilling, is a procedure in which fat taken from one part of the body is processed and injected into another to restore volume or improve contour.[1] Under the eyes it is used to fill the tear trough, the hollow groove where the lower eyelid meets the cheek, so that the transition from eyelid to cheek looks smoother, the shadowing is reduced and the face looks more rested and youthful.[2][3]

A 2024 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery describes fat loss from specific facial fat compartments as a major contributor to the aged look, and presents fat grafting as a way to restore that volume. It divides grafts by particle size into macrofat, microfat and nanofat: the first two mainly add volume, while nanofat, an emulsified preparation, has been reported to improve skin texture and pigmentation.[2] Proponents of nanofat for the under-eye area value it because it can be placed in thin, superficial skin, and because it contains adipose-derived stromal cells that a 2021 review links to tissue remodeling.[4]

Research specific to the tear trough is limited, but small randomized trials have compared nanofat with platelet-rich plasma for infraorbital dark circles.[5] Forum users on looksmax.org have discussed lipofilling in the under-eye region mostly through topical products and fillers, while surgical fat grafting appears in the surgical and injectable end of under-eye options.[6]

chain: Fat harvested from the body and processed
Placed in the tear trough or as nanofat in thin under-eye skin
Hollow and shadow soften, skin may look smoother
angle.text: Fat grafting adds volume to the under-eye hollow, which reduces the shadowed step between lower lid and cheek. Nanofat is used in the thinnest skin and is reported to improve skin quality and pigmentation as well.

paras: The procedure has three stages: harvesting fat, often by liposuction, processing it, and injecting it into the target area.[1] Sources describe minimizing handling and re-injecting promptly to preserve graft survival.[1] Harvest and preparation methods, including cannula size and filter cartridges, determine whether the result is macrofat, microfat or nanofat.[2]

Nanofat is produced by mechanically emulsifying fat until it passes through fine filters, giving a fluid that can be injected with very thin needles into superficial layers. A 2021 review describes it as a compact bundle of stromal cells with regenerative and tissue remodeling potential.[4]

Lower-eyelid surgery addresses fat protrusion, skin laxity and the eyelid-cheek contour, and adjunctive midface fat repositioning is sometimes used to smooth the transition between lid and cheek.[7] Fat grafting is an alternative or complement for patients whose main concern is hollowing rather than excess tissue.[2][7]

Besides facial volume restoration, fat grafting is used in other regions such as the breast, and a 2021 paper on periorbital fat grafting by Marten and Elyassnia is among the references on Wikipedia's fat-transfer page.[1]

Listed complications include swelling, bruising, hematoma, paresthesia or donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and injury from cannulas.[1] Fat necrosis and reabsorption are recognized concerns; Wikipedia cites reabsorption of up to about 50 percent in breast augmentation.[1]

Separately, an overview of injectable fillers states that rare blindness and delayed skin necrosis can follow embolization of injected material, and that necrosis is more often linked to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.[8]

A 2023 single-blinded randomized comparative trial in Dermatologic Surgery compared platelet-rich plasma with autologous fat transfer using nanofat for infraorbital dark circles.[5] A 2024 randomized trial of stromal vascular fraction, PRP and a Q-switched laser added to nanofat-treated dark circles and wrinkles under the eyes was later retracted by its journal.[9]

Other nanofat trials have addressed acne scars, wound healing, burn wounds and breast-reduction scars rather than the tear trough.[10][11] A completed phase 2/3 registration (NCT01461785, n=25, started 2012) evaluated activated platelet-rich plasma in human autologous fat transfer, a related but different question.[12] A 2013 report described basic research and early clinical use of nanofat grafting.[13]

timeline.event: Nanofat grafting is described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, with basic research and clinical applications.[13]
A World Journal of Stem Cells review surveys nanofat preparation methods and regenerative applications.[4]
Randomized trial compares PRP with nanofat fat transfer for infraorbital dark circles.[5]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery review distinguishes macrofat, microfat and nanofat for facial rejuvenation.[2]
